trial_allocation.allocation_rationale: Baseline model — fixed defaults, no HPO needed.

Lasso has a small search space (primarily alpha). 4 trials are sufficient to explore a range of regularization strengths given the modest feature count (24) and large sample size (4604). More trials would yield diminishing returns.

Random forest has moderate complexity (n_estimators, max_depth, min_samples_split). With 4604 samples, 6 trials allow exploration of key parameters without excessive computational cost. It is less sensitive to hyperparameters than boosting.

Gradient boosting (sklearn) has moderate sensitivity to learning_rate, n_estimators, and max_depth. 6 trials provide a fair search given that it shares the boosting concept with xgboost but is often slower to converge.

XGBoost is the most promising model for low MAE on this dataset, but it has the largest and most sensitive hyperparameter set (n_estimators, learning_rate, max_depth, subsample, colsample_bytree, regularization). 8 trials are allocated to thoroughly explore its search space within the 30-trial budget.

SVR with RBF kernel requires tuning of C and gamma, but training time per trial is higher due to quadratic complexity. 6 trials balance the need to find good parameters with the risk of excessive runtime. Its expected performance is lower than boosting, so it receives fewer trials than xgboost.

checklist.comment: All selected models (ridge, lasso, random_forest, gradient_boosting, xgboost, svr) are appropriate for regression tasks.
Ridge serves as a linear baseline, which is acceptable. A trivial baseline (e.g., mean predictor) could be added for stronger reference.

30 total trials across 5 HPO models (lasso, random_forest, gradient_boosting, xgboost, svr) averages only 6 trials each. This is likely insufficient for effective hyperparameter tuning, especially for ensemble models.
k-fold cross-validation is suitable for 4604 samples. The primary MAE metric is appropriate for regression.
Evaluation metric (MAE) and primary metric (MAE) are consistent and correctly applied for a regression task.
With a small HPO budget, the risk is more about inadequate tuning than severe overfitting. Some models may underfit or fail to reach optimal generalization if hyperparameters are not well explored.
SVR may be computationally heavy, but with only ~6 trials and moderate data size, resource consumption is expected to be manageable.
No random seed is specified for model initialization, data splits, or HPO sampling. This can lead to non-deterministic results and hinder reproducibility.

non_blocking_risks.message: Allocating only 30 total trials across 5 HPO-enabled models severely limits hyperparameter exploration, potentially yielding suboptimal model configurations.
non_blocking_risks.suggested_action: Increase max_total_trials to at least 100-200 or use early stopping/pruning to allocate trials more efficiently. Consider prioritizing fewer models for HPO.

non_blocking_risks.message: Absence of a fixed random_state across models, data splits, and HPO sampler may lead to non-reproducible results.
non_blocking_risks.suggested_action: Set a global random seed (e.g., random_state=42) for all stochastic components to ensure repeatable experiments.

future_improvement_suggestions: Add a trivial baseline (e.g., DummyRegressor predicting mean/median) to provide a lower-bound performance reference.
Specify the number of folds (k) in cross-validation to make the evaluation explicit (commonly 5 or 10).
Consider enabling early stopping for iterative models (gradient_boosting, xgboost) to reduce runtime and overfitting risk.
Document the HPO search spaces for each model to facilitate review and reproducibility.
